Pregnancy

Epilepsy, fertility and planning a pregnancy

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Having epilepsy does not rule out becoming a parent. The useful question is how to plan conception and care around your particular epilepsy and treatment. A coordinated review can address fertility concerns, protect seizure control and explain medicine-related risks without promising either a risk-free pregnancy or inevitable harm.

Epilepsy does not rule out becoming a parent

Many people with epilepsy have children, and most pregnancies in people with epilepsy result in a healthy baby. The diagnosis alone does not tell you whether conception will be difficult. Seizure patterns, particular medicines, reproductive health and other circumstances all matter. Planning offers an opportunity to review these factors without assuming that everyone needs fertility treatment.

A 2018 prospective study followed 89 women with epilepsy and 108 women without epilepsy who were seeking pregnancy. Pregnancy rates and time to conception were similar. The participants had no previous infertility-related disorder, so this reassuring finding does not settle every individual fertility problem. It challenges a blanket assumption of reduced fertility rather than guaranteeing a quick pregnancy.

Arrange a joint review before trying to conceive

Ask your epilepsy specialist and maternity or preconception team to review the plan together, preferably before contraception is stopped. Bring the exact medicine names, doses, supplements, recent seizure history and any rescue plan. Discuss previous treatment failures, troublesome adverse effects and what support you would need during pregnancy. The aim is a workable plan that protects both seizure control and reproductive health.

Decisions should reflect your priorities and a clear explanation of the available options. A change may be worthwhile before conception, but even apparently mild epilepsy does not make stopping treatment automatically safe. Some medicines have specific pregnancy-prevention requirements. Agree on suitable contraception while a needed review or carefully supervised change is completed, including when it is appropriate to try for pregnancy.

Irregular periods deserve their own assessment

Tell the clinician about missed or infrequent periods, changes in bleeding patterns or difficulty conceiving. These can reflect several causes rather than epilepsy alone. Some medicines, including valproate, can affect reproductive function. A medication review and an appropriate reproductive-health assessment can help identify what is relevant; do not stop an antiseizure medicine or start hormone treatment yourself.

One possible explanation is the hormonal condition traditionally called polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, in current NHS information. It can involve irregular ovulation, excess androgen effects and metabolic problems. The name does not mean that ovarian cysts alone establish the diagnosis. Neither epilepsy nor an irregular cycle proves that this condition is present.

Fertility concerns also matter for men

Men with epilepsy can become fathers. Changes in sexual desire, erections or fertility should be discussed rather than attributed automatically to the diagnosis. The exact medicine and other health factors matter. Effects on reproductive function vary by medicine; symptoms and difficulty conceiving need an individual assessment.

Valproate product information includes reports of impaired male fertility, with improvement reported in some people after treatment was reduced or stopped. That does not establish that stopping it will restore fertility for everyone, and a person should not try this without specialist supervision. Ask whether a fertility assessment and a safer treatment plan are appropriate. Fertility effects and possible risks to a future child are separate questions.

Separate inheritance from medicine exposure

The chance of a child developing epilepsy depends partly on the parent’s epilepsy type and underlying cause. Some forms have a genetic contribution; others are associated with an acquired brain injury or another condition. A diagnosis in a parent does not mean that a child will necessarily have epilepsy. A specialist can explain whether genetic counselling would be useful for the particular family.

This inherited susceptibility is different from the effects of a medicine taken during pregnancy. Some antiseizure medicines increase the chance of particular birth defects or later developmental difficulties, but risks differ by medicine, dose and treatment combination. Developmental outcomes also vary between children. Neither an exposure nor a family history determines an individual child’s outcome, and one general percentage cannot answer all of these questions.

Choose treatment for the epilepsy as well as the pregnancy

Maintaining control of convulsive seizures is an important part of protecting the pregnant person and baby. The specialist considers which medicines actually work for the seizure type, previous responses and other health conditions. The 2024 AAN, AES and SMFM guideline recommends considering options such as lamotrigine, levetiracetam or oxcarbazepine when clinically appropriate to reduce birth-defect risk; none is a universal substitute or a guarantee of no risk.

If a switch is needed, planning it before conception gives time to assess seizure control and tolerability. Removing an effective treatment after pregnancy has begun can introduce substantial risk, especially when it controls convulsive seizures. Do not lower a dose, omit tablets or copy another person’s regimen. A useful consultation compares the risks of the proposed medicine with the risks of inadequately treated epilepsy.

Valproate requires a specific maternal-risk discussion

Valproate, including sodium valproate and valproic acid, has well-established risks of birth defects and developmental problems when used during pregnancy. Current UK product information restricts its use for epilepsy in pregnancy to situations where no suitable alternative exists. For people who could become pregnant, UK pregnancy-prevention safeguards apply. The local specialist should explain the applicable rules, alternatives and why a particular plan is being recommended.

Risk can vary with dose and exposure, but there is no established dose that removes all fetal risk. Folic acid does not cancel valproate’s risks. If pregnancy occurs while taking it for epilepsy, contact the specialist urgently and keep taking the prescribed treatment until the team gives an individualized plan. Abrupt withdrawal can provoke serious seizures; an urgent review is not an instruction to stop at home.

Paternal valproate evidence is different and remains uncertain

Research has examined whether valproate taken by men around conception could affect a child’s neurodevelopment. In June 2026, the European Medicines Agency reviewed inconsistent findings and concluded that a causal role remained uncertain. This is not the same evidence as the established risks from maternal use during pregnancy, and it should not be described as either proof of harm from fathers or proof of no risk.

The European precautionary measures remained in place. Current UK advice includes effective contraception during treatment and for at least three months after stopping, using condoms together with contraception used by the female partner, and no sperm donation during that period. Men planning fatherhood should discuss treatment with their specialist before changing it. Local requirements can differ; the review should cover the current advice where care is provided.

Check topiramate precautions and contraceptive interactions

Topiramate also needs a specific pregnancy discussion. UK measures introduced in 2024 require a pregnancy-prevention programme for people who can become pregnant, including highly effective contraception during treatment and for at least four weeks after stopping. For epilepsy during pregnancy, it should be used only when there is no suitable alternative. A person taking it for epilepsy who suspects pregnancy needs urgent specialist advice and should not stop it independently.

The reason for treatment matters: instructions for topiramate used for migraine prevention are different. Contraception also needs a medicine-by-medicine check. Some antiseizure medicines can reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, while estrogen-containing contraception can lower lamotrigine levels. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to check the exact combination before starting, stopping or changing contraception; a method that suits someone else may not suit your regimen.

Agree on folic acid rather than copying a dose

Folic acid should be discussed before conception, with the dose chosen for the medicine plan and local guidance. The 2024 US AAN, AES and SMFM guideline recommends at least 0.4 mg daily before and during pregnancy for people taking antiseizure medication. UK NICE guidance recommends 5 mg daily before pregnancy and through the first 12 weeks for higher-risk situations, including medicines that affect folate. These are named guideline approaches, not doses to add together.

Ask the team which product and dose to use and how long to continue it; bring any prenatal vitamin so the total is clear. Folate is important but cannot prevent every birth defect. It can lower phenytoin levels in some circumstances, so starting or stopping it may require coordinated monitoring. Phenytoin and folic acid can be used together with an appropriate plan: neither withholding folate nor adjusting the seizure medicine yourself is the solution.

A positive pregnancy test needs prompt contact

If pregnancy was not planned, contact the epilepsy and maternity teams promptly, and urgently if there is no pregnancy treatment plan or you take a medicine with pregnancy restrictions. Give the medicine names and doses and explain when the pregnancy test became positive. Continue the prescribed antiseizure treatment while obtaining advice. An exposure is a reason for careful assessment, not a prediction that the pregnancy must have a poor outcome.

Tell the team urgently if vomiting prevents you from keeping medicine down, or if seizures change or become more frequent. Do not improvise extra doses after vomiting; ask for product-specific instructions. The team can review treatment, arrange appropriate antenatal assessment and explain available screening. Keep a written contact plan so a routine appointment delay does not leave you without advice.

Monitoring is individualized during pregnancy

Pregnancy can alter medicine levels, particularly for treatments such as lamotrigine and levetiracetam. Depending on seizure risk and the drug, the specialist may compare blood levels with a pre-pregnancy baseline and adjust treatment. A level is interpreted alongside symptoms and seizure control, not as a number to act on alone. Report missed doses, adverse effects and new seizures rather than waiting for the next planned review.

Antenatal care may include a detailed fetal ultrasound and additional monitoring selected for the medicine exposure or other findings. Ask what each test can detect and what it cannot rule out. A reassuring scan cannot exclude every later developmental difference. Keep follow-up after birth as advised, including discussion of a child’s development when there has been exposure to antiseizure medication.

Plan delivery, feeding and the first weeks at home

Epilepsy does not automatically require a caesarean birth. The maternity and epilepsy teams should agree on medicine timing, seizure management and the most appropriate birth setting. Discuss feeding choices with the exact medicine list: breastfeeding advice depends on the treatment and circumstances. Ask what changes in the baby should prompt contact with the clinical team.

The weeks after birth can bring disrupted sleep and missed-dose risks. Arrange practical help, reminders and a plan for safe infant care. If doses increased during pregnancy, the team may need to reduce them after birth as medicine handling changes; agree on this before delivery and follow the written schedule rather than returning to an old dose independently. Ongoing specialist review remains important even when pregnancy and birth went well.

Know which seizure changes are emergencies

Call emergency services for a first seizure, a seizure lasting longer than usual, or one lasting more than five minutes when the usual duration is unknown. Also seek emergency help if the person does not recover as usual, has another seizure before recovering, has difficulty breathing or is seriously injured. Follow an established individualized emergency plan if one is available; a new seizure during pregnancy needs emergency assessment rather than being assumed to be ordinary epilepsy.

While waiting, protect the head from injury, move nearby hazards and time the seizure. Do not restrain the person or put anything in their mouth. After convulsions stop, place them on their side and stay with them; do not give food or drink until they have fully recovered. Only a person trained to follow the prescribed rescue plan should give rescue medicine.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring the complete medicine list and seizure history to a joint preconception review. Ask about fertility concerns, inheritance, contraception and any supervised treatment change before trying to conceive.

Agree on folic acid, pregnancy monitoring and a plan for vomiting or missed medicine. Check jurisdiction-specific valproate and topiramate precautions with the treating team.

Before delivery, confirm medicine and feeding advice, practical support and any planned postpartum dose adjustment. Keep emergency and urgent-contact instructions accessible.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize medicine lists, seizure notes and questions for the care team. It cannot choose or change antiseizure treatment, estimate an individual genetic risk or replace specialist and emergency care.

When to seek help

Do not stop, reduce or switch antiseizure medicine yourself. Seek urgent advice for an unexpected pregnancy without a plan, vomiting that prevents medicine retention or changed seizures. Call emergency services for a first, prolonged or repeated seizure without recovery, failure to recover normally, breathing difficulty or serious injury.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Many people with epilepsy have healthy pregnancies; fertility and inherited risk require individual assessment.
  • Review treatment before conception when possible, and never stop or reduce an antiseizure medicine on your own.
  • Maternal valproate risks are established; evidence about paternal valproate exposure remains uncertain, with precautions still in place.
  • Folic acid and contraception should be selected for the exact medicines and current local guidance.
  • Keep an urgent-contact plan for pregnancy, vomiting or changed seizures, and an emergency plan for prolonged or repeated seizures.

Frequently asked questions

Can epilepsy or its treatment affect a future baby?

Some epilepsy types have an inherited contribution, and some medicines taken during pregnancy increase the chance of birth defects or developmental difficulties. These are different risks. The particular diagnosis, medicine, dose and family history matter; many people with epilepsy have healthy children.

Why should I not stop treatment after a positive pregnancy test?

Uncontrolled seizures can harm you and the pregnancy, and suddenly stopping an effective medicine can provoke serious seizures. Contact the epilepsy and maternity teams promptly, urgently for a restricted medicine or no existing plan. Continue the prescribed treatment while a specialist advises on the safest next step.

Does epilepsy explain my irregular periods?

Not necessarily. Medicines and hormonal or other reproductive conditions can contribute. Report missed or irregular periods and difficulties conceiving so the clinician can assess the cause. A diagnosis of epilepsy alone does not establish PMOS, formerly called PCOS, or infertility.

Can antiseizure medicines affect male fertility?

Some can, and valproate product information describes reports of impaired male fertility. Improvement after changing treatment has been reported but is not guaranteed. Do not assume that every medicine has the same effect or stop treatment yourself; ask for an individualized medication and fertility assessment.

Will my child inherit epilepsy?

Not necessarily. The chance depends on the epilepsy type and its underlying cause. Discuss family history and the exact diagnosis with the specialist; genetic counselling may help when an inherited form is suspected. A general population figure cannot determine the risk for one family.

Should everyone with epilepsy take the same folic acid dose?

No. The US guideline recommends at least 0.4 mg daily before and during pregnancy for people taking antiseizure medication; UK guidance uses 5 mg before pregnancy and through the first 12 weeks for specified higher-risk situations. Ask your team which approach applies, including any phenytoin monitoring. Do not combine these doses or assume folate removes all medicine-related risk.

Does the 2026 paternal valproate review mean precautions can stop?

No. The EMA found inconsistent evidence and an uncertain causal link, but retained precautions. Current UK advice includes contraception during treatment and for at least three months after stopping, and no sperm donation in that period. Review fatherhood plans with the specialist rather than stopping medicine or precautions independently.

When is a seizure an emergency?

Call emergency services for a first seizure, one longer than usual or over five minutes if the normal duration is unknown, repeated seizures without recovery, failure to recover as usual, breathing difficulty or serious injury. Follow the individual emergency plan. Vomiting that prevents medicine retention or changed seizures during pregnancy also requires urgent clinical advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
